title: Get Smart!: How to Think and Act Like the Most Successful and Highest-Paid People in Every Field
author: Brian Tracy
summary:
Get Smart! is Brian Tracy's argument that intelligence, in the sense that actually predicts success, is less about raw IQ and more about a learnable set of thinking habits that most people simply never develop. Tracy opens with a provocative framing: the average person uses only a small fraction of their mental capacity, and the people who seem naturally brilliant are usually just using more of what everyone already has, through specific, repeatable patterns of thought rather than innate advantage.

The book moves through a series of practical mental disciplines rather than abstract cognitive theory. Early chapters focus on reframing how the reader relates to their own thinking capacity — using an extended metaphor of an inaccessible bank account to illustrate how much unused potential most people carry — before moving into structured tools for applying that capacity more effectively. Central to this is the GOSPA model, a goal-oriented planning framework (Goals, Objectives, Strategies, Plans, Activities) that Tracy presents as a way of forcing the "slow-thinking," deliberate part of the brain to do the strategic work that the fast, reactive mind tends to skip.

A significant portion of the book addresses obstacles to clear thinking rather than only techniques for it — most notably a chapter on negative emotions (fear, envy, resentment, jealousy, inferiority, hate, suspicion, hostility, distrust) that Tracy argues actively degrade decision-making quality by narrowing attention and triggering reactive rather than deliberate thought. He also introduces the "Seven Rs of Superior Thinking" — rethinking, reevaluating, reorganizing, restructuring, reengineering, reinventing, and regaining control — as a repeatable checklist for approaching stuck problems from new angles rather than repeating the same failed approach.

Throughout, Tracy grounds the material in familiar business contexts: idea validation through research and expert consultation, systematic problem-solving methods, and disciplined goal-setting, drawing on decades of his own consulting and speaking experience with successful individuals across fields. The book's throughline is that thinking well is a trainable skill with identifiable components — perspective, planning discipline, emotional regulation, and structured reevaluation — rather than a fixed trait, and that consistently applying these components, even simple ones, compounds into a meaningfully different quality of decision and outcome over time.

sections.title: Change Your Perspective
sections.summary:
The opening chapter reframes the reader's basic assumption about their own intelligence, using the extended metaphor of a bank account containing a fortune of which only a tiny fraction is accessible — a stand-in for unused mental capacity most people carry without realizing it.

Tracy argues that people who appear exceptionally capable are typically not working with more raw potential, but are simply accessing more of what's already available through specific habits of attention and thought. The chapter challenges the reader's internalized story about being "less smart" than admired peers, positioning the rest of the book as a set of tools for closing that access gap rather than a claim that anyone needs to become a different kind of person.

The chapter hands off to the following material by promising specific, learnable techniques rather than further motivational reframing alone.
keyLessons: Perceived intelligence gaps between people are often gaps in mental habits and access, not raw capacity.
Reframing your relationship to your own thinking is a necessary first step before specific techniques become useful.

sections.title: The GOSPA Planning Model
sections.summary:
This chapter introduces GOSPA — Goals, Objectives, Strategies, Plans, Activities — as a structured planning sequence meant to slow down decision-making enough for the deliberate, "slow-thinking" part of the brain to do real strategic work rather than defaulting to the fast, reactive mind.

Tracy walks through each stage of the model with a worked example, showing how a vague ambition becomes progressively more actionable as it moves from broad goal to specific daily activities. He is explicit that skipping stages — jumping straight from a goal to activities without objectives or strategy in between — is a common failure pattern that produces busy but ineffective effort.

The chapter connects to the following chapters on emotional obstacles by noting that even a good model like GOSPA breaks down when negative emotion or reactive thinking interferes with using it consistently.
keyLessons: The GOSPA sequence (Goals, Objectives, Strategies, Plans, Activities) forces deliberate strategic thinking rather than jumping straight to busy activity.
Skipping planning stages between a goal and daily activity is a common cause of effort that doesn't translate into results.

sections.title: Managing Negative Emotions
sections.summary:
This chapter directly addresses the emotional obstacles to clear thinking: fear, envy, resentment, jealousy, feelings of inferiority, hate, suspicion, hostility, and distrust. Tracy argues these states aren't just unpleasant but functionally degrade decision quality by narrowing attention onto threat and grievance rather than opportunity and strategy.

He works through several of these emotions individually, describing how each one typically arises and offering specific reframing or interruption techniques — for example, treating envy as useful information about what you actually want rather than something to suppress or feel guilty about. The chapter is notably candid about how common and normal these emotions are, positioning the goal as management rather than elimination.

The chapter transitions into the following material on systematic problem-solving by arguing that a calmer emotional baseline is a prerequisite for the more structured thinking techniques that follow.
keyLessons: Negative emotions like fear, envy, and resentment narrow attention and degrade decision quality by triggering reactive rather than deliberate thinking.
Naming and examining a negative emotion (like envy) for the information it contains is more useful than simply suppressing it.

sections.title: Systematic Problem Solving
sections.summary:
This chapter lays out a repeatable method for approaching problems methodically rather than relying on intuition alone: clearly defining the actual problem, gathering relevant information, generating multiple possible solutions before committing to one, and testing assumptions before large commitments of time or money.

Tracy emphasizes research and consulting others with relevant expertise as an underused step — arguing that many failed ventures could have been caught earlier through basic outside validation that founders skip out of overconfidence or urgency. He illustrates this with the kind of due-diligence example a reader might apply to evaluating a new product or business idea.

The chapter hands off to the "Seven Rs" material by framing systematic problem-solving as most valuable precisely when a first approach has already failed and a fresh angle is needed.
keyLessons: Defining the actual problem precisely, before jumping to solutions, prevents wasted effort on the wrong fix.
Seeking outside expert input before large commitments is a frequently skipped but high-value step in idea validation.

sections.title: The Seven Rs of Superior Thinking
sections.summary:
This chapter introduces a structured checklist — rethinking, reevaluating, reorganizing, restructuring, reengineering, reinventing, and regaining control — as a tool for approaching a stuck situation from genuinely new angles rather than repeating the same failed approach with more effort.

Tracy walks through what each "R" specifically prompts a reader to examine, ranging from questioning basic assumptions (rethinking) to considering whether an entire approach needs to be abandoned and replaced (reinventing). The chapter's underlying argument is that most people, when stuck, intensify their existing approach rather than questioning whether the approach itself is the problem.

The chapter closes by connecting this checklist back to the GOSPA model from earlier, suggesting the Seven Rs as a diagnostic tool to apply when a GOSPA-planned effort has stalled.
keyLessons: Being stuck usually calls for questioning the approach itself, not simply applying more effort to the existing approach.
The Seven Rs checklist (rethink, reevaluate, reorganize, restructure, reengineer, reinvent, regain control) gives a structured way to generate a genuinely new angle on a stalled problem.

sections.title: Continuous Learning and Growth Opportunities
sections.summary:
This chapter addresses the long-term habit of treating every situation, including setbacks, as containing usable information and opportunity — a disposition Tracy argues distinguishes consistently successful people from others facing similar circumstances.

He discusses deliberate practices for ongoing learning (reading, seeking feedback, studying people who are ahead in a given area) and argues that opportunity recognition itself is a trainable skill, sharpened by consistently asking what a difficult situation might be revealing or making possible rather than only what it's costing.

The chapter hands off to the closing material on decisive action by arguing that learning without follow-through has limited value on its own.
keyLessons: Treating setbacks as sources of usable information, not just costs, is a trainable habit that compounds over time.
Opportunity recognition sharpens with deliberate practice, not just experience alone.

sections.title: Deciding and Acting with Precision
sections.summary:
The closing chapter addresses the gap between good thinking and actual results, arguing that even excellent planning and emotional management fail to produce outcomes without decisive, well-timed action.

Tracy discusses common patterns of decision avoidance — over-researching, waiting for certainty that will never arrive, and diffusing responsibility across a group rather than owning a call — and offers criteria for recognizing when enough information exists to act. He closes the book by tying this back to the opening bank-account metaphor: unused thinking capacity only matters once it's converted into action.

The book ends here, positioning decisive action as the practical culmination of every mental discipline introduced earlier in the book.
keyLessons: Over-researching or waiting for certainty is itself a common form of decision avoidance, not genuine diligence.
Mental capacity and planning only produce results once converted into decisive, well-timed action.
Perceived gaps in intelligence between people are usually gaps in thinking habits and access, not raw mental capacity.
The GOSPA sequence (Goals, Objectives, Strategies, Plans, Activities) prevents busy effort that never converts into real progress.
Negative emotions like fear, envy, and resentment measurably degrade decision quality by narrowing attention onto threat.
Naming a difficult emotion for the information it contains, rather than suppressing it, is more useful for clear thinking.
Defining a problem precisely before jumping to solutions prevents wasted effort solving the wrong issue.
Seeking outside expert validation before large commitments is a frequently skipped, high-value diligence step.
Being stuck usually calls for questioning your entire approach, not just applying more effort to the existing one.
Decisive, well-timed action is what converts thinking capacity into actual results.

quotes.text: The average person uses only about two percent of their mental ability.
quotes.attribution: description of Brian Tracy's central claim in *Get Smart!*

quotes.text: Think before you act — know yourself — decide what your future is going to be like.
quotes.attribution: paraphrased core guidance described by a reader of *Get Smart!*

conceptsFrameworks.name: The GOSPA Model
conceptsFrameworks.definition: A structured planning sequence — Goals, Objectives, Strategies, Plans, Activities — designed to slow decision-making down enough for deliberate strategic thought to occur, preventing the common failure of jumping straight from a vague goal to unfocused activity.

conceptsFrameworks.name: The Seven Rs of Superior Thinking
conceptsFrameworks.definition: A diagnostic checklist — rethinking, reevaluating, reorganizing, restructuring, reengineering, reinventing, and regaining control — used to approach a stalled or stuck situation from a genuinely new angle rather than intensifying a failing existing approach.
conceptsFrameworks.sourceSection: The Seven Rs of Superior Thinking

actionSteps: Take one current vague goal and run it explicitly through the GOSPA sequence, writing out objectives, strategies, plans, and specific activities rather than jumping straight to a to-do list.

The next time you notice envy or resentment toward someone else's success, write down specifically what it reveals about something you actually want, rather than dismissing or suppressing the feeling.
Before your next significant decision or commitment, deliberately seek out one person with relevant outside expertise to validate or challenge your assumptions.
When you feel stuck on a specific problem this week, run it through the Seven Rs checklist one at a time rather than simply trying harder at your current approach.
reflectionQuestions: Where in your life have you been assuming a fixed limit on your own capability that might actually be a gap in habits rather than capacity?
Is there a decision you've been delaying under the guise of "more research" that may actually be avoidance of committing to a call?
Which negative emotion — fear, envy, resentment, or another — most often narrows your thinking in a specific recurring situation?

points: Several readers and reviewers of the book note that much of its core advice on goal-setting and planning overlaps heavily with Tracy's own earlier, more focused books (particularly on goal-setting), so a reader already familiar with his other work may find limited new material here.

The claim that "the average person uses only about two percent of their mental ability" is a popularized and scientifically unsupported framing (a version of the debunked "10% of the brain" myth); Tracy's broader point about underused thinking habits is more defensible than this specific figure, which should not be taken as an established neuroscience finding.

Some reader reviews describe portions of the book as offering fairly generic advice already common in the self-help and productivity space, rather than original research-backed insight, and at least one reviewer reported abandoning the book early for this reason.

As with much of Tracy's work, claims about "decades of research" behind the techniques are asserted rather than cited to specific, checkable studies, making it difficult for a reader to verify the empirical basis independently.

whoThisIsFor: Readers who want a practical, structured set of thinking and planning habits (goal-setting, emotional regulation, problem-solving) in an accessible, business-audience format.
whenToReadThis: When you feel stuck in a specific goal or decision and want a structured framework (like GOSPA or the Seven Rs) to think through it differently, rather than simply trying harder at your current approach.

authorBio.name: Brian Tracy
authorBio.bio:
Brian Tracy is a Canadian-American self-development author, speaker, and business consultant, and chairman and CEO of Brian Tracy International. Over several decades he has consulted with more than a thousand companies and delivered thousands of talks and seminars internationally on personal effectiveness, sales, and management.

He is one of the most prolific authors in the business self-help category, having written dozens of books that consistently emphasize goal clarity, disciplined planning, and personal responsibility as the drivers of success, most famously in *Eat That Frog!*. *Get Smart!*, published in 2016, extends this focus specifically into the mechanics of thinking and decision-making.

sourceNotes:
Synthesis is based on publisher descriptions, reader reviews, and third-party chapter/content summaries of *Get Smart!* gathered via web search, including specific documented references to the GOSPA model, the Seven Rs of Superior Thinking, and the chapter on negative emotions; exact original chapter numbering and titles beyond these documented elements were not independently confirmed, so some chapter titles here are constructed around the verified thematic content rather than quoted from an original table of contents. Quotes were kept to a small, verified set given a thin public quote footprint for specific verbatim passages, consistent with the copyright-safe limits noted at the top of this file. The "two percent of mental ability" claim is flagged in Critical Take as a popularized figure without a solid scientific basis, based on general, well-established knowledge about brain-usage myths.
